alt: Misrepresentation makes a contract voidable: it stands until the innocent party chooses to set it aside. An operative mistake usually makes it void: it was never a contract. The difference matters most when goods have been sold on to an innocent third party.
caption: Misrepresentation: voidable. Operative mistake: void.

alt: A misrepresentation is an untrue statement of fact that induces the contract. 1: a statement, by words or conduct (Spice Girls); silence generally is not (Fletcher v Krell) except half-truths, changed circumstances and utmost good faith. 2: of fact, not opinion (Bisset v Wilkinson), though expert opinion (Esso v Mardon) and lies about present intention (Edgington) count. 3: inducement: no reliance after the claimant’s own check (Attwood v Small), but failing to check does not matter (Redgrave v Hurd).
caption: Test each element with a case: statement, fact, inducement.

after: ## The three types and their remedies
alt: Fraudulent misrepresentation (Derry v Peek) gives rescission and damages in deceit for all direct losses (Doyle v Olby). Negligent misrepresentation under s 2(1) gives rescission and damages measured as if fraudulent (Royscot), and the maker must prove reasonable belief (Howard Marine v Ogden). Negligent misstatement at common law (Hedley Byrne) gives damages in tort. Innocent misrepresentation gives rescission, or damages instead under s 2(2). Section 3 subjects exclusion clauses to the UCTA reasonableness test.
caption: The type decides the remedy; s 2(1) puts the burden on the maker of the statement.

alt: Rescission sets the contract aside and restores the parties, but as an equitable remedy it is lost by affirmation (Long v Lloyd), undue delay (Leaf v International Galleries), impossibility of restitution (Clarke v Dickson), or an innocent third party acquiring rights for value.
caption: Rescission is lost by affirming, delaying, being unable to give back, or third-party rights.

alt: Under the 1945 Act damages can be reduced where the claimant was partly at fault. Damages under s 2(1) can in principle be reduced where the defendant was also liable in negligence (Gran Gelato v Richcliff, though no reduction was made), but contributory negligence is no defence to fraud (Standard Chartered v Pakistan National Shipping).
caption: A careless claimant may lose some damages for negligent misrepresentation, never for fraud.

alt: Common mistake: both parties make the same mistake, operative for non-existent subject matter (Couturier v Hastie) or res sua (Cooper v Phibbs) but almost never for quality (Bell v Lever Bros; Great Peace). Mutual mistake: cross-purposes, as with the two ships Peerless (Raffles v Wichelhaus) and hemp or tow (Scriven v Hindley). Unilateral mistake: one party is mistaken and the other knows, as to terms (Hartog v Colin and Shields) or identity, void in writing (Cundy v Lindsay; Shogun) but voidable face to face (Phillips v Brooks; Lewis v Averay).
caption: Same mistake, cross-purposes, or one side mistaken and the other aware.

alt: When a rogue uses a false identity, a written contract is usually void because the named party’s identity is vital (Cundy v Lindsay; Shogun Finance v Hudson). Face to face, the seller is presumed to deal with the person in front of them, so the contract is only voidable (Phillips v Brooks; Lewis v Averay), with Ingram v Little treated as exceptional.
caption: In writing, identity is vital and the contract is void; face to face, it is only voidable.

alt: Bilal’s statement "it makes £800 a week" is a statement of fact that became untrue and was not corrected (With v O’Flanagan). Sana relied on it, and failing to check does not matter (Redgrave v Hurd). As Bilal knew the truth it is fraudulent (Derry v Peek), or at least s 2(1). She can claim rescission and damages, with no reduction for carelessness if it is fraud (Standard Chartered), provided she acts promptly and does not affirm (Long v Lloyd).
caption: IRAC each element: statement, fact, inducement, type, remedy, bars.
